questions.problem: The radius of a circle is increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the circle is numerically equal to one third of the rate of increase of the diameter. Determine the radius of the circle at that moment.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$  be the radius, $A$ the area, and $D$ the diameter of the circle. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{3}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the diameter $D$ of the circle. Since $D=2r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $D$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{D}{2})}^{2}=\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}D}(\frac{\pi {D}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\pi D}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{3}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\pi D}{2} \\ \frac{1}{3} & =\frac{\pi D}{2} \\ D & =\frac{2}{3\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $D=2r,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2r & =\frac{2}{3\pi } \\ r & =\frac{1}{3\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}9\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi } \\ 9 & =\frac{C}{2\pi } \\ C & =18\pi .\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi r & =18\pi  \\ r & =9.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =2\cdot 9 \\ D & =18.\end{aligned}

questions.problem: The radius of a circle is increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the circle is numerically equal to two-thirds of the rate of increase of the circumference. What is the radius of the circle at that moment?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$  be the radius, $A$ the area, and $C$ the circumference of the circle. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi } \\ \frac{2}{3} & =\frac{C}{2\pi } \\ C & =\frac{4\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $C=2\pi r,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi r & =\frac{4\pi }{3} \\ r & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Water leaking onto a floor forms a circular puddle. The area of the puddle increases at a rate of $40\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{2}\text{/min}.$ How fast is the radius of the puddle increasing at the moment when the radius is $5\text{ cm}?$
questions.worked_solution:
In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=5,$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=40\pi .$

To start, let's write down the area formula for the circle and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=40\pi $ and $r=5,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}40\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi (5) \\ 40\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 10\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the radius is increasing at a rate of $4$ centimeters per minute.

In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=6,$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-24\pi .$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

When $r=6\,\text{km},$ $C=2\pi (6)=12\pi \text{ km}.$ Hence, substituting $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-24\pi $ and $C=12\pi $, and solving for $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-24\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{12\pi }{2\pi } \\ -24\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot 6 \\ \frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{24\pi }{6} \\ \frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =-4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the circumference is decreasing at a rate of $4\pi \text{ km/year}.$

A giant inflatable ball is losing air uniformly, causing its radius to change at a rate of $\frac{1}{12\pi }\,\text{in}\text{/s}.$ If the radius at a certain moment is $24\,\text{in},$ what is the rate at which the surface area is decreasing?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $A$ its surface area. Both $r$ and $A$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{12\pi }\,\text{in}\text{/s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=24\,\text{in}.$

To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}8\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{12\pi }$ and $r=24.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{12\pi }\cdot 8\pi (24) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-16.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the surface area of the ball is decreasing at a rate of $16{\text{ in}}^{2}\text{/s}.$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the snowball and let $A$ be its surface area. Both $r$ and $A$ change with time. In particular, we are given that

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{5}\,\text{in/s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ when $A=100\pi \,{\text{in}}^{2}.$

To start, let's write down the formula for the surface area of a sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 8\pi r\end{aligned}
$$

We then calculate the value of $r$ using $A=100\pi .$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ 100\pi  & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ 25 & ={r}^{2} \\ r & =\pm 5\end{aligned}
$$

Since radius cannot be negative, we have $r=5.$

We now substitute $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{5}$ and $r=5$ into our expression for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{5}\cdot 8\pi \cdot 5 \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-8\pi \end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the surface area of the snowball is decreasing at a rate of $8\pi \,{\text{in}}^{2}\text{/s}.$

Let $r$ be the radius of the hailstone and $A$ its surface area. Both $r$ and $A$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{6\pi }\,\text{mm}\text{/s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=15\,\text{mm}.$

To start, let's write down the surface area formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =4\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}8\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{6\pi }$ and $r=15.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{6\pi }\cdot 8\pi (15) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-20.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the surface area of the hailstone is decreasing at a rate of $20{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$

A spherical balloon is being inflated, causing its enclosed volume to increase at a rate of $128\pi \text{ }{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.$ How fast is the radius increasing at the moment when the radius is $4\text{ }\text{cm}?$ Do not round the answer.

The radius of the balloon is increasing at a rate of 
{{field-1}} $\text{cm}/\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=128\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=4\,\text{cm}.$

To start, let's write down the formula for the volume of a sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=128\pi $ and $r=4,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}128\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi (4)^{2} \\ 128\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 64\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when the radius of the balloon is $4\,\text{cm},$ the radius is increasing at a rate of $2$ $\text{ }\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.$

and we want to find $r$ when $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=\frac{3}{4\pi }\text{ cm/s}.$

$$

canonical_examples.problem: The radius of a circle is increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the circle is numerically equal to half the rate of increase of the circumference. What is the radius of the circle at that moment?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $r$  be the radius, $A$ the area, and $C$ the circumference of the circle. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\textrm d C}{\textrm d t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A = \pi r^2,$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A =  \pi r^2 =  \pi \left(\dfrac{C}{2\pi} \right)^2 = \dfrac{C^2}{4\pi}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\textrm d C}{\textrm d t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi } \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{C}{2\pi } \\ C & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $C = 2\pi r,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi r & =\pi  \\ r & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
A circular oil spillage is being cleaned up by a team using specialized cleaning equipment. If the area of the circle is *decreasing* at a rate of $6\pi\,\text{m}^2/\text{h}$, what is the rate at which the radius is decreasing at the instant when the radius is $2\,\text{m}?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14065925/assets/d769569ed7854f4d6eb085853b51eb0e5aab0e14cfc3bcdf1e5a480d996ccc9e.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
In this situation, we want to find $\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d t}$ at the moment when $r=2,$ and we are also told that  $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = -6\pi.$

To start, let's write down the area formula for the circle and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm dA}{\textrm dt} = -6\pi$ and $r=2,$ and solve for $\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi (2) \\ -6\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the radius is decreasing at a rate of $\dfrac{3}{2}$ meter per hour.

canonical_examples.problem:
Air is leaking from a spherical balloon at the rate of $500\pi\,\text{cm}^3/\text{s}.$ How fast is the radius of the balloon decreasing when the radius is $10\,\text{cm}?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14065925/assets/460fd4059be2c655e01b89db2738225a50578b5c76bbe048f83312f0bff655ec.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt} = -500\pi\,\text{cm}^3/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt}$ when $r=10\,\text{cm}.$

To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt} = -500\pi$ and $r=10,$ and solve for $\dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-500\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi (10)^{2} \\ -500\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 400\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{5}{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-1.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of the balloon is decreasing at a rate of $1.25\,\text{cm}/\text{s}$ when the radius is $10\,\text{cm}.$
